title: Gurmukhi on screens
hookLine: the Granth is now searchable online, with translations

lines: ONE HYMN, TWO ENDS OF A SCREEN.
cards: At the back of a gurdwara, a girl leans toward her grandfather and whispers: what's that line? The ragis are singing, and she can't quite catch it. He doesn't open a book.

He points at the wall, where a screen shows the line in Gurmukhi, then the same sounds in Roman letters, then a meaning in English. He reads the top line. She reads the bottom two, mouthing the words.
For a moment they're singing the same hymn from different ends of the screen.

teach.h: READ BY ANG, THE SAME PAGES.
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib is read by ang, the word Sikhs use for its pages. Printed copies keep the same page layout, which is why these lessons can send you to one ang and you'll find the same hymn there.
Today the whole Granth can be searched on a phone or a website.
Some tools let you type just the first letter of each word, so a half-remembered line can still be found.
In some gurdwaras, the line being sung goes up on a screen with a transliteration and a translation, so someone who can't read Gurmukhi can follow along. One careful step, though.
Sikhs treat the Gurmukhi as the Guru's own word.

A translation underneath is a helper: one person's reading, made with care, but not the Guru. Different translations sometimes disagree, and that's a reason to go back to the top line, not away from it.
At Ang 982, Guru Ram Das says it plainly: bani guru, guru hai bani.
The Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar.
For Sikhs who hold that, a screen that carries the Word into the back row can be a kind of seva: a lamp moved closer to people who couldn't see. Not a replacement for the Granth. A way to reach it.

how: Sikhs use websites and apps to search the Guru Granth Sahib by ang or by the first letters of a line, and some gurdwaras project the hymn being sung in Gurmukhi with a transliteration and a translation.

games.q: you're in the back row of a gurdwara and can't follow the Gurmukhi being sung. what does today's story offer?
o: nothing; you're meant to know it already.
the line on a screen, with sounds and meaning.

games.why: the screen shows the Gurmukhi, then a transliteration, then a translation. a girl and her grandfather sing the same hymn from different ends of it.

practice: If you have a screen nearby, open any ang of the Guru Granth Sahib and pick one line; if not, use today's: bani guru, guru hai bani.
Breathe in with the first half and out with the second, and sit with what it means, the Word is the Guru, without hurrying to the next line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at the end.

wordCard.voice: Gurmukhi. The script of the Guru Granth Sahib, now searchable online and shown on screens with transliteration and translation, so more people can reach the Word itself. Today's word.
